annotations.annotation_text: Page 287 opens Book 2, Chapter 2 ("The Night Lessons") during the Age of Heroes phase. This passage continues the children studying the Trivium and Quadrivium, Dolph and Kev drawing geometric diagrams of ALP's body, marginal glosses and footnotes, featuring Shem (Dolph), Shaun (Kev), Issy (footnotes). The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.
sources: Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp
McHugh, Roland. Annotations to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/annotationstofin0000mchu_h5g8
Gordon, John. Finnegans Wake: A Plot Summary. https://johngordonfinnegan.weebly.com
JJDA: Finnegans Wake Genetic Edition. https://jjda.ie

annotations.annotation_text: ALP invocation "alp" on page 287 ("The Night Lessons"): Anna Livia Plurabelle, the mother-river personifying the Liffey, surfaces here amid the children studying the Trivium and Quadrivium, Dolph and Kev drawing geometric diagrams of ALP's body, marginal glosses and footnotes. In this Age of Heroes passage, her feminine current of forgiveness and renewal flows through the dream landscape, carrying Dublin's history from source to sea.
sources: Bishop, John. Joyce's Book of the Dark. https://archive.org/details/joycesbookofdark0000bish
Hart, Clive. Structure and Motif in Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/structuremotifin0000hart

annotations.annotation_text: Mid-page polysemic node on page 287 ("The Night Lessons"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Heroes dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
